blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A plan may fund at most 2 of the substation projects S1 to S5, written as one row on their sum, and S3 is a must-do project. What does the row allow?

options.text: One substation project besides S3, since S3 takes one of the 2 places
options.says: Right: the must-do row fixes x_S3 at 1, so it takes one of the 2 the sum allows, as P017 does under every transmission cap.

options.text: Two substation projects besides S3, since a must-do sits outside the count
options.says: The sum includes x_S3, and the must-do row sets it to 1; nothing removes it from the count.

options.text: No plan at all, since a must-do inside a capped sum is a conflict
options.says: The rows conflict only when the cap is smaller than the must-dos in the group, such as a cap of 0 here.

options.text: Any two projects of the five, since the must-do row gives way to the cap
options.says: Every row holds at once; neither gives way, so S3 is always one of the two.

origin.section: A Counting Row Caps How Many Projects of One Kind Are Funded

questions.stem: A regulator asks that projects in the Ridge region make up at most 30% of the projects a plan funds. Which row states that rule in a MILP?

options.text: Ridge's count is at most 0.3 times the number of candidate projects
options.says: The share is of the funded projects; a constant from the candidate list lets Ridge take most of a small plan.

options.text: Ridge's count divided by the plan's count is at most 0.3
options.says: Dividing by an expression of the variables is not linear; multiply both sides out first.

options.text: Ridge's count is at most 0.3 times the plan's count
options.says: Right: the plan's count is never negative, so the ratio can be multiplied out into one linear row.

options.text: Ridge's count is at most 0.3, since every share lies between 0 and 1
options.says: A count is a number of projects, not a share; this row would allow no Ridge project at all.

origin.section: A Counting Row Caps How Many Projects of One Kind Are Funded

questions.stem: A crane hire covers up to 4 pole replacements and costs $50k. A planner writes the hires as a continuous variable h of at least 0, with 4h at least the number of replacements funded, and charges 50h to the budget. What does the model charge for a plan with 5 replacements?

options.text: 2 hires, $100k, since the row rounds the count up to whole hires
options.says: Only an integer domain rounds up; a continuous h may stop at exactly 5/4.

options.text: 1 hire, $50k, since the solver rounds h down to save budget
options.says: h = 1 breaks the row 4h >= 5; the solver never rounds a variable against a row.

options.text: 5 hires, $250k, since each replacement needs a hire of its own
options.says: The row is 4h >= 5; one hire covers up to 4 replacements, so 5 hires are never needed.

options.text: 1.25 hires, $62.5k, less than the $100k the crane firm will bill
options.says: Right: a continuous h buys a quarter of a hire, as m = 1.333 did for GridCap's mobilizations.

origin.section: A Count Rounded Up to Whole Batches Needs an Integer Variable
